pages.text: A student in Bolgatanga presses a switch and the room fills with light. The electricity doing that work may have been made a moment earlier at Akosombo, at Bui, or at Aboadze on the coast, hundreds of kilometres away. It crossed forests, rivers, and savanna on wires hung from tall steel towers, and it arrived almost at once. Along the way its voltage was raised to a level that would kill instantly and then lowered again to a level a home can use. Why go to all that trouble? The answer is about saving energy.

Along the way its voltage was raised to a level that would kill instantly and then lowered again to a level a home can use.
Why go to all that trouble?
The answer is about saving energy.
pages.alt: A map of Ghana with power stations marked in the south and lines of pylons running north to Bolgatanga.

pages.text: The journey starts in a power station, where turbines spin generators. The generators produce electricity at several thousand volts. Before it leaves, it passes through a transformer, a device that changes voltage. A step-up transformer raises the voltage to 161,000 volts or even 330,000 volts. The electricity then travels along thick cables carried by steel towers called pylons. Together, the power stations, lines, and transformers that cover the country form the national grid. In Ghana, the high-voltage lines are run by a company called GRIDCo. Almost none of the electricity is stored on the way: it is used at the moment it is made.

The electricity then travels along thick cables carried by steel towers called pylons.
Together, the power stations, lines, and transformers that cover the country form the national grid.
In Ghana, the high-voltage lines are run by a company called GRIDCo.
Almost none of the electricity is stored on the way: it is used at the moment it is made.
pages.alt: A power station beside a large transformer, with thick cables rising to the first of a line of pylons.

pages.text: Here is the reason for the high voltage. When a current flows through a wire, the wire becomes warm, and that heat is wasted energy. A larger current wastes much more. Now, electrical power is voltage multiplied by current. So the same power can be sent in two ways: a low voltage with a large current, or a high voltage with a small current. Raise the voltage 25 times and the current needed falls to one twenty-fifth. With so small a current, the long wires stay cool and very little energy is lost on the journey.

So the same power can be sent in two ways: a low voltage with a large current, or a high voltage with a small current.
Raise the voltage 25 times and the current needed falls to one twenty-fifth.
With so small a current, the long wires stay cool and very little energy is lost on the journey.
pages.alt: Two wires side by side: one glowing warm and carrying thick arrows, the other cool and carrying thin arrows.

pages.text: Such voltages are far too dangerous for a town. So near the end of the journey the electricity enters a substation, where step-down transformers lower the voltage. Distribution companies such as ECG in the south and NEDCo in the north carry it along streets at 33,000 or 11,000 volts. Finally, a transformer on a pole or in a fenced yard near your home lowers it to 230 volts for your sockets. The hum you hear from that grey box is the transformer at work. Even 230 volts can kill, so sockets and wires must still be treated with respect.

pages.text: Why can a bird sit on a bare wire? Current flows only when there is a difference in voltage to drive it. Both of the bird’s feet are on the same wire, at the same voltage, so almost no current passes through its body. If the bird touched a second wire, or a wire and the pole together, it would complete a circuit and die. People are in far greater danger, because we stand on the ground. A person who touches a live wire offers the current a path to earth through the body.

pages.text: The signs showing a lightning flash mean what they say. Never climb a pylon or enter a substation. Never fly a kite, raise a ladder, or carry a long metal pole near overhead lines. Never build, sell, or play under high-voltage lines. Stay far from any wire that has fallen, and report it. Illegal connections kill people every year and start fires that destroy markets and homes. Pay for what you use and let trained workers do the wiring. Electricity is a good servant that has travelled a long way to reach you. Do not let it become a dangerous master.

activities.question: What does a step-up transformer do?
options: It stores electricity for the night

activities.question: Why is electricity sent across the country at a very high voltage?
options: The current is smaller, so less energy is wasted as heat in the wires
Pylons work only at high voltage

activities.question: Why is a bird on a single wire not harmed?
options: The wire is covered with thick rubber
Both feet are at the same voltage, so almost no current flows through the bird

activities.question: Apply it: A neighbour offers to connect your house to the pole himself to avoid paying. Using the article, what is the best response?
options: Refuse: illegal connections cause deaths and fires; ask the power company
Accept, but only in the dry season

activities.prompt: Follow electricity from the dam to your room. Put the stages in order.
items: A generator in the power station produces electricity
A step-up transformer raises the voltage
High-voltage lines on pylons carry it across the country
A substation lowers the voltage for the town
A transformer near your home lowers it to 230 volts
